title: 10. Security & Auth: API Keys

objectives: What is the fundamental difference between an API key and a JWT?
Why must API keys never be exposed in browser-side JavaScript?
How do you rotate an API key with zero downtime?
Should API keys be stored in plaintext in the database?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** API keys are simple opaque secret strings issued by a service to a client (typically another service or a developer) that authenticate and identify the caller on each request, usually sent in a header, and validated by a server-side lookup against a registry that maps each key to a scope, owner, and revocation state.

API keys are the oldest and simplest form of machine-to-machine authentication on the web. They predate OAuth 2.0, JWT, and OIDC by more than a decade — the original Flickr API (2004), AWS access keys (2006), and Stripe's secret keys (2011) all used variants of the same idea: give the developer a long random string, have them paste it into a header or query parameter on every request, and look it up server-side. Three decades later the pattern is still everywhere because, for service-to-service traffic where the caller is a piece of code rather than a user, an opaque key is often exactly the right tool. It avoids the complexity of OAuth flows, requires no token endpoint, no JWKS, no signature verification, and no clock skew handling. The server simply receives the key, hashes it, looks it up in a database, and either accepts or rejects the call.

The critical difference between an API key and a JWT is what the token does *not* contain. A JWT carries signed claims — issuer, subject, audience, expiry, scopes — that the server can verify offline without any database lookup. An API key carries nothing: it is just a random string, and every meaningful property (who owns it, what it can do, when it expires, whether it has been revoked) lives in the server's key registry. This makes API keys stateful in the verification sense (you must hit the registry on each call, or a cache of it) but stateless in the token sense (the token is just bytes). The trade-off is straightforward: JWTs are self-validating but hard to revoke before `exp`; API keys can be revoked instantly by flipping a row in the database, but every call must pay the lookup cost. For high-volume internal traffic, teams usually wrap the registry lookup in a Redis cache with a 30-second TTL — long enough to absorb the per-request cost, short enough that revocation propagates within a minute.

Real-world API key systems all converge on a small set of best practices. Stripe publishes two kinds of keys: a *publishable* key (`pk_live_...`) that is safe to expose in browser JavaScript because it can only create tokens for cards, and a *secret* key (`sk_live_...`) that can charge cards and must never leave the server — they are visually distinguished by prefix so developers and code scanners can tell which is which. AWS issues an access key ID (`AKIA...`, semi-public, used to identify the key in logs) and a secret access key (the actual secret, used to sign requests via HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical request). GitHub personal access tokens (PATs) are prefixed `ghp_...` for classic tokens, `github_pat_...` for fine-grained tokens, and `gho_...` for OAuth tokens — the prefix lets GitHub's secret-scanning feature detect leaked tokens in commits and auto-revoke them. All three providers enforce scoping (Stripe: restricted keys with permission lists; AWS: IAM policies attached to the key; GitHub: scopes on classic tokens, per-repository permissions on fine-grained tokens), rotation (AWS lets you have two active keys per IAM user for zero-downtime rotation), and revocation (one click in the dashboard, propagates within seconds).

The single most important rule with API keys is that they must never be exposed client-side in a public context. A key in browser JavaScript is effectively public — anyone can open DevTools, read the key, and reuse it. Stripe's publishable keys exist precisely because some operations (tokenizing a card in the browser) must be done client-side, and the only safe way to do that is to issue a key that is intrinsically limited to those operations. The same rule applies to mobile apps: an API key embedded in an APK or IPA can be extracted, so mobile clients should either use a backend-for-frontend that holds the key, or use a flow that mints short-lived tokens (OAuth 2.0 PKCE, App Attest, Firebase App Check). The principle is: **the longer-lived and more powerful the secret, the closer to the server it must live.** A long-lived key with full account access belongs only in environment variables on a server you control; a short-lived scoped token with read-only access to one resource may, with care, be exposed to a client.

Rotation is the second practice that separates mature key systems from amateur ones. Every long-lived secret must be replaceable without downtime. The standard pattern is to allow a key's owner to have two active keys simultaneously: the old key (about to be rotated out) and the new key (just generated). The operator deploys the new key to all services, watches logs to confirm no traffic is using the old key, and then revokes the old one. AWS, Stripe, and GitHub all support this two-key rotation pattern. For emergency rotation — a leaked key, a departing engineer — the operator revokes immediately and accepts the brief downtime, then redeploys with a new key. The compensating control is audit logging: every API call records the key ID used, so a leaked key's blast radius can be reconstructed after the fact. Stripe's dashboard shows the last 30 days of requests by key, AWS CloudTrail logs every API call with the access key ID, and GitHub's audit log records every PAT usage. Without audit logs, you cannot answer the question "what did this key do before we revoked it?" — and that question is mandatory in any incident response.

Finally, API keys must be transmitted securely and stored hashed. Transmitting a key over plain HTTP means any network observer (coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a compromised router) can read and replay it — so HTTPS is mandatory, and HSTS prevents the first-request downgrade. Storing keys in plaintext in the database means a SQL injection or a database dump leaks every customer's key at once; storing them hashed (like passwords, with a slow KDF or at least SHA-256 + per-key salt) means a leak exposes only hashes that must be brute-forced. The lookup pattern is: receive key, hash with the same algorithm, look up the hash in the registry, retrieve the row. AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, and Stripe's internal key store all follow this pattern. The key ID (the non-secret prefix) is stored in plaintext and used for logging; the secret portion is stored only as a hash. This separation is what allows logging `ak_live_...ABC` (the last four chars) in audit logs without exposing the secret.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Developer requests API key] --> B[Service generates random secret]
    B --> C[Hash secret + store row: key_id, hash, owner, scopes, exp, revoked]
    C --> D[Return plaintext key once to developer]
    D --> E[Developer puts key in server env var]
    E --> F[Client service sends request: Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...]
    F --> G[Server hashes incoming key]
    G --> H[Lookup hash in key registry]
    H --> I{Found and not revoked?}
    I -- No --> J[Reject 401]
    I -- Yes --> K[Check scopes cover requested operation]
    K -- No --> J
    K -- Yes --> L[Check rate limit + audit log]
    L --> M[Process request]
    M --> N[Record key_id in audit log]
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+-----------+   1. POST /v1/keys    +-----------+
| Developer | --------------------> | Key       |
| (CLI)     |                       | Service   |
+-----------+                       +-----+-----+
      ^                                    |
      | 2. return sk_live_abc123           | 3. store
      |    (shown ONCE)                    |    hash(sk) + meta
      v                                    v
+-----------+                       +-------------+
| Server    | <-------------------- | Key Registry|
| env var   |   lookup by hash      | (DB/Redis)  |
| sk_live_..|                       +-------------+
+-----+-----+                              ^
      |                                    | 4. verify
      | request: Authorization: sk_live_.. |    hash match
      v                                    |    revoked? exp?
+-----------+                              |
| API       | -----------------------------+
| Gateway   |
+-----+-----+
      |
      | 5. scopes include "charges:write"?
      v
+-------------+
| Allow or 403|
+-------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. A developer (or a service automation pipeline) requests a new API key from the key service, specifying the owner, the requested scopes (e.g., `charges:write`, `customers:read`), and an optional expiry.
2. The key service generates a long random secret (typically 32 bytes, base64url-encoded to ~43 chars), prepends a prefix that identifies the key type and environment (e.g., `sk_live_` for Stripe-style live secret key), hashes the secret with SHA-256, and stores a row containing the key ID, the hash, the owner, the scopes, the expiry, and `revoked=false`.
3. The plaintext key is returned to the developer exactly once and shown on screen; the developer stores it in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Doppler) or a server-side environment variable — never in source control, never in browser code.
4. On each request, the client sends the key in a header (`Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...` or `X-API-Key: sk_live_...`); the API gateway or service hashes the incoming secret, looks it up in the registry (with a Redis cache in front for hot paths), and rejects with 401 if the hash is missing or the key is revoked or expired.
5. If the key is valid, the server checks whether the key's scopes cover the requested operation (a key with `customers:read` cannot call `POST /charges`), then checks the rate limit for the key, records the key ID and operation in the audit log, and processes the request.
6. To rotate, the developer creates a second key, deploys it across all services, watches the audit log until no traffic uses the old key, then sets `revoked=true` on the old key — the cache TTL (typically 30–60 seconds) means stale traffic drops within a minute.

quiz.explanation: An API key is an opaque random string whose meaning lives entirely in the server's registry: every property — owner, scopes, expiry, revocation state — is looked up on each call. A JWT is a self-contained, signed token that carries those claims inside it and can be verified offline with the issuer's public key, requiring no database hit.

quiz.explanation: Anything in browser JavaScript is effectively public — any user can open DevTools, read the key, and reuse it from anywhere on the internet. A long-lived server key in browser code lets an attacker impersonate the account, read all accessible data, and run billable operations until the key is rotated.

quiz.explanation: Prefixes serve three jobs. First, they identify the key type and environment at a glance — sk_live_ is a Stripe live secret key, pk_test_ is a test publishable key, ghp_ is a GitHub classic PAT, AKIA... is an AWS access key ID. Second, they enable secret scanning: GitHub, GitGuardian, and TruffleHog scan commits for known prefixes and can auto-revoke leaked keys within minutes.
